description: Rock 'n' roll, the counterculture, feminism, Stonewall, and American society transformed.
content_html:
Rock ‘n’ Roll and the Teenagers of the 1950s

In the early 1950s a new musical form emerged from the fusion of African American rhythm and blues with country music. When Elvis Presley recorded “That’s All Right” in Memphis in 1954, rock and roll had its first mainstream star. Presley’s swivelling hips and uninhibited stage style scandalised parents and conservative commentators — he was initially shown only from the waist up on television. Rock and roll sold to white teenagers music rooted in Black culture, contributing to a gradual cultural integration, though the original Black artists — Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Fats Domino — were often paid less and reached smaller audiences than their white counterparts.

Key Fact

Rock and roll emerged in the mid-1950s, with Elvis Presley its most visible white star. It challenged racial barriers (fusing Black and white musical traditions) and generational norms (celebrating youth rebellion). Television — which reached nearly 90 per cent of American homes by 1960 — gave rock and roll national reach and created the first true teenage mass market.

The 1960s Counterculture

By the mid-1960s, a broader counterculture had emerged among young Americans. The “hippie” movement rejected materialism, the Vietnam War, and conventional social norms. Young people gathered at events like the Woodstock music festival in August 1969 — attended by approximately 400,000 people — as a celebration of peace, music and alternative values. Student protests against the Vietnam War spread to campuses across the country; at Kent State University, Ohio, in May 1970, National Guardsmen shot and killed four students during a protest, shocking the nation.

In the early hours of 28 June 1969, police raided the Stonewall Inn, a gay bar in New York City’s Greenwich Village. Instead of submitting to arrest as had been customary, the patrons — many of them transgender women, drag queens and homeless youth — fought back. The Stonewall uprising lasted several days and galvanised the gay rights movement. The first Pride march in New York took place in June 1970. By the 1980s and 1990s, gay rights organisations had become a significant force in American politics, though the AIDS crisis of the 1980s devastated gay communities and highlighted ongoing discrimination in healthcare and government responses.

Second-Wave Feminism

The women’s movement underwent a revival in the 1960s and 1970s. Betty Friedan’s influential 1963 book The Feminine Mystique argued that middle-class American women were trapped in a domestic role that left them unfulfilled. In 1966, Friedan co-founded the National Organization for Women (NOW) to campaign for equal rights. Second-wave feminism made significant legal gains: the Equal Pay Act (1963) mandated equal pay for the same work; the Civil Rights Act (1964) banned sex discrimination in employment; Roe v Wade (1973) established the constitutional right to abortion.

Key Fact

Key legal milestones for women’s rights: Equal Pay Act (1963), sex discrimination banned under the Civil Rights Act (1964), and Roe v Wade (1973) legalising abortion nationwide. However, the proposed Equal Rights Amendment (ERA), passed by Congress in 1972, was never ratified by the required number of states, blocked in part by a conservative backlash organised by activist Phyllis Schlafly.

Media, Entertainment and Cultural Change, 1950–2000

Television transformed American culture from the 1950s onwards. By the 1980s, MTV (launched August 1981) was reshaping the music industry by creating a visual dimension to popular music and making image as important as sound. Hip hop, emerging from New York’s Black and Latino communities in the late 1970s, grew from local party music into one of the world’s most commercially successful genres by the 1990s, carrying messages about urban poverty, police brutality and racial identity to mainstream audiences.

The 1990s brought the internet into American homes. The World Wide Web became publicly accessible in the early 1990s, and by 2000 around 50 per cent of US households had internet access. Online retail, email and digital media began to transform commerce, communication and entertainment — setting the stage for the social media revolution of the twenty-first century. The 1990s technology boom also drove the economic expansion that characterised the Clinton years, though the “dotcom bubble” burst in 2000 wiping out trillions of dollars of stock market value.
exam_tip_html: For 8-mark “Explain Change” questions on American society, show specific evidence of change at the start and end of the period — e.g. the role of women in 1950 compared with 1980 after Roe v Wade and NOW campaigns. Avoid vague language like “things improved” — use precise evidence. For 16-mark essays on social change, the examiners expect you to weigh whether change was genuine and lasting, or limited and contested (ERA failed; abortion rights contested; gay rights limited before 1990s).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rock and roll in the 1950s and the 1960s counterculture challenged mainstream American values, crossing racial and generational boundaries. The Stonewall uprising (1969) launched the modern gay rights movement.
  • Second-wave feminism won significant legal gains — Equal Pay Act (1963), sex discrimination ban (1964), Roe v Wade (1973) — but the Equal Rights Amendment was never ratified, showing the limits of feminist change.
  • Media transformation from 1950s television to MTV (1981) to the internet by 2000 reshaped American culture. Hip hop brought urban Black American voices into the mainstream. The 1990s technology boom drove economic growth but ended in the dotcom crash of 2000.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the 1960s counterculture in the USA.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names feature (rejection of materialism; opposition to Vietnam War; the hippie movement; the Woodstock festival) AND develops it. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the second-wave feminist movement in the USA (1960s-1970s).
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. (1) It campaigned for legal equality and organisations like NOW led lobbying campaigns that achieved the Equal Pay Act (1963) and the ban on sex discrimination in the Civil Rights Act (1964); (2) Roe v Wade (1973) established the constitutional right to abortion, a major victory for reproductive rights activists. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the emergence of the counterculture in the USA in the 1960s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cause (opposition to Vietnam War; post-war prosperity creating leisure time for young people; influence of civil rights movement; rock and roll creating a youth culture separate from adults) AND develops through a chain of reasoning. Secure: Cause with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Stonewall uprising of 1969.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (galvanised gay rights movement; led to first Pride marches in 1970; creation of gay rights organisations; growing political visibility leading to eventual legal recognition decades later) AND develops the chain of effects. Secure: Consequence with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Roe v Wade (1973) for the development of American society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (established constitutional right to abortion; a major feminist victory; changed the relationship between women and the state over reproductive decisions) AND over time (remained deeply contested; became a key political battleground; conservative movement worked for decades to overturn it, eventually succeeding in 2022 in Dobbs v Jackson). Secure: One time frame well-covered. Developing: Describes Roe without analysing significance. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'American society changed more between 1950 and 1975 than between 1975 and 2000.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs the pace of change in both periods. 1950-75 arguments (civil rights legislation; women's rights gains; youth counterculture; rock and roll; Stonewall). 1975-2000 arguments (MTV and media transformation; internet revolution; hip hop; gay rights visibility and AIDS crisis; end of Cold War). Substantiated judgement. Secure: Clear argument on both sides. Developing: Describes changes without weighing relative significance. Emerging: Narrative.

right: A proposed constitutional amendment for gender equality passed by Congress in 1972 but never ratified
A genre fusing Black rhythm and blues with country music, the soundtrack of 1950s teenage rebellion
A 1960s social movement rejecting mainstream values and opposing the Vietnam War

flashcard_questions.q: Who was the most prominent white star of 1950s rock and roll?
When was the Woodstock music festival?
What happened at the Stonewall Inn on 28 June 1969?
flashcard_questions.a: Police raided a gay bar; patrons fought back, sparking the gay rights movement.

flashcard_questions.q: What organisation did Betty Friedan co-found in 1966?
What did the Equal Pay Act (1963) require?
flashcard_questions.a: Equal pay for men and women doing the same work.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Roe v Wade (1973) establish?
What was the Equal Rights Amendment?
flashcard_questions.a: A proposed constitutional amendment guaranteeing equal rights regardless of sex; passed by Congress in 1972 but never ratified.
New York's Black and Latino communities in the late 1970s.
A technology stock market boom of the late 1990s that crashed in 2000, wiping out trillions in value.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the counterculture's attitude to the Vietnam War?
flashcard_questions.a: Strongly opposed; anti-war protest was a central feature of 1960s counterculture.

glossary_terms.definition: A genre combining African American rhythm and blues with country music, which became the soundtrack of 1950s youth culture and a symbol of generational rebellion.
A social movement of the 1960s that rejected mainstream American values, embraced alternative lifestyles, experimented with drugs, and opposed the Vietnam War.
The 1969 uprising at the Stonewall Inn in New York City, regarded as the catalyst for the modern gay rights movement.
The feminist movement of the 1960s-1970s that campaigned for equal rights in employment, education, reproductive rights and legal equality, building on the first wave of suffragette campaigning.
A proposed constitutional amendment that would have guaranteed equal rights regardless of sex, passed by Congress in 1972 but never ratified by enough states to become law.
The cable television channel launched in 1981 that brought music videos to a mass audience, reshaping the music industry and creating new celebrity cultures.
